bibliographic.title: We are Building Gods: AI as the Anthropomorphised Authority of the Past
bibliographic.citation_apa: Öhman, C. (2024). We are building gods: AI as the anthropomorphised authority of the past. Minds and Machines, 34(8). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-024-09667-z

methodology.method_family: philosophical and conceptual analysis with critical-theoretical illustration (Martin Hägglund)
methodology.technology_context: large language models, ChatGPT, LLM chatbots

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article is a peer-reviewed conceptual-theoretical essay arguing that LLMs should be interpreted as anthropomorphised authority of the past, with normative critique of bias, unpredictability, privacy, and democratic freedom. It mentions LLMs and chatbots but, in the text provided, does not examine conversational governance mechanisms, operational controls, audit/observability, compliance implementation, or LLM deployment in regulated high-stakes environments.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only partial front-matter text was supplied (mainly pages 1-2; page 9 truncated), so later sections on governance implications, limitations, and full argument cannot be fully verified.

appraisal.notes: Appraisal adapted for a non-empirical conceptual paper. Sampling and data-collection criteria are not applicable. Rigor and limitations scores are conservative because only partial text was available.

cerqual.explanation: The argument presented in the available text is internally coherent and clearly stated, but its adequacy and relevance to conversational governance in regulated LLM systems is limited because the work reframes LLMs philosophically rather than analysing governance practices, oversight architectures, or regulated-sector deployments.

coding.theme: Philosophical reconceptualization of LLMs as personified collective authority
coding.subtheme: Religious and anthropological metaphor applied to ChatGPT/LLM critique
concepts: stochastic synthesis of past speech acts
rq_alignment: conceptual framing of authority and accountability in LLM-mediated interaction

synthesis.main_claim: LLMs should be understood not as quasi-divine cognition, but as anthropological gods: personified authorities synthesised from traces of past human speech, which users may falsely experience as extra-human and thereby tempt democratic abdication to a tyranny of the past.
synthesis.contribution: Offers a theological/anthropological metaphor and mobilises religious critique, illustrated through Martin Hägglund, to reinterpret LLM risks beyond bias and unpredictability toward spiritual and democratic freedom.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence for normative and conceptual discussions of LLM authority, anthropomorphism, and democratic accountability; not as central evidence on operational conversational governance, guardrails, observability, audit, or regulated-environment implementation.
